protections: P1: decrypted vault content written to a file must be created owner-only (0600); the earlier guard is a process-wide os.umask(0o077) in the ansible-vault CLI (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:145-146, restored at 242-243) plus mkstemp for the edit temp (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:853).

P2: the file that receives decrypted content must stay the same securely-created inode; it must not be unlinked and re-opened by name, or another local user can interpose a file/symlink (mkstemp at lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:853 versus os.remove+open at 1076-1082).
P3: decrypted temporary files must be destroyed after use (_shred_file at lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:815-846, called at 865 and 872).
P4 (must keep working): re-encrypting/editing an existing vault file preserves the destination's mode/ownership (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:1094-1097 and 1020-1022).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: ansible-vault sets umask 0o077 before running the action and the edit temp comes from mkstemp, so temp/output files are already owner-only; nothing needs to change in the library.
mkstemp already created the temp file with a random name and mode 0600 in a sticky /tmp, so refilling that same temp file cannot be read or redirected by another local user.

DataLoader writes the decrypted vault data through the mkstemp fd (mode 0600) and only unlinks it at cleanup, so it is not the racy remove/reopen pattern; a fix aimed at ansible-vault edit need not touch this second implementation.
If reading or encrypting the edited data fails the command aborts, so a leftover plaintext file is harmless; the editor-error and no-change paths already shred the temp file.

The bytes shuffle_files/rekey_file put in place are already ciphertext, and restoring the destination's mode and ownership is deliberate; a blanket 0600 rule here would silently change the users' file modes.

masking: The earlier hardening (umask 0o077 at lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:146 and mkstemp at lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:853) masks the residual defect: because the temp file is created 0600, the unlink+recreate at lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:1076-1082 no longer looks like an insecure-temp-file problem, so the mode loss and the race window are easy to overlook.

conflicts.what: Forcing 0600 on every file that write_data recreates collides with shuffle_files/rekey_file restoring the destination's mode and ownership (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:1094-1097, 1020-1022); the owner-only rule has to be scoped to plaintext writes only.

Closing the temp race with O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW on every open would break the supported symlink-following behaviour of encrypt/decrypt/edit (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:904, 913, 942, 989; tests at test/units/parsing/vault/test_vault_editor.py:289-304, 362-395).

fairness_risks: A blanket 'all vault files must be 0600' rule contradicts the must-keep-working mode/ownership preservation for encrypted destinations (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:1094-1097, 1020-1022).

Refusing symlink destinations (O_NOFOLLOW) breaks encrypting/decrypting/editing a vault file through a symlink, which is supported and tested (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:904, 913, 942, 989 and the 'follow the symlink' comments; test/units/parsing/vault/test_vault_editor.py:289-304, 362-395).

The '-' stdout pseudo-filename and special paths such as /dev/null must keep working (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:887-891, 1073-1074; test/units/parsing/vault/test_vault_editor.py:480-492); a rule that chmods or refuses non-regular outputs would break them.

An unchanged edit must leave the encrypted file byte-identical (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:870-873; test/units/parsing/vault/test_vault_editor.py:169-186); a fix must not re-encrypt or shred the destination on that path.

design.why: Four independent fix sites. T1+T2 are one shared-guard group (the CLI-only umask and the write_data unlink/reopen in the same write path): the deepseek-trap is that the umask/mkstemp story sounds complete, while the library entry points and the recreated inode are not covered. T3 is a second implementation of 'decrypt vault data to a temp file' that a fix aimed only at ansible-vault would miss. T4 is the absent cleanup route that only exists after the editor returns. T5 is the mimo-type coupled value: over-hardening every mode to 0600 breaks the deliberate mode/ownership preservation, so the solver must scope the rule to plaintext. This mix needs four separate judgements instead of one blanket permissions change.

unverified: The exact diff of the 2022 fix commits (77d0effcc5b2, 84afa8e90cd1, ffd3757fc354) could not be read: the sandbox has no shell/git and the object database is outside the permitted path, so the residual sites were derived from the pinned code only.

Whether the earlier fix introduced the os.umask(0o077) block (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:145-146) or the mkstemp temp (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:853) cannot be attributed from the worktree; both guards are present in the pinned code.

Related but not counted: the persistent-connection control directory is created without an explicit mode (lib/ansible/cli/scripts/ansible_connection_cli_stub.py:261-262, default ~/.ansible/pc in lib/ansible/config/base.yml:1639-1646) and the AF_UNIX socket is bound without chmod (lines 108-109); that is the same 'expose resource to wrong sphere' family but belongs to a different advisory.
_shred_file resolves 'shred' through PATH (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:833), an untrusted-search-path concern outside CWE-362/377/668 and not counted.

ansible-vault encrypt_string accepts --output (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:66, 96-97) but execute_encrypt_string never writes output_file; this is a functional gap, not a temp-file exposure, and is not counted.
